Measurement definitions & limits

Shape difference is 100 × (1 − intersection-over-union) of aligned masks. Asymmetry is the average fraction missing after reflection across two principal axes. Color difference is mean CIELAB distance between overlapping pixels after subtracting surrounding skin color. These are experimental image measurements, not clinical ABCDE scores. No medical thresholds or disease classifier are used. Camera angle, hair, lighting, makeup, skin tone, segmentation errors, and image scale can affect every measurement.

Physical size is deliberately not estimated: these photos have no validated millimeter reference. Equal-area normalization removes growth information. A low difference does not establish safety.

EXPLAINABLE BY DESIGN

Small model. Visible decisions.

All photo processing happens on this device. No account, API key, or GPU is needed.

01

Learn the photo's colors

A deterministic k-means model groups sampled pixels into four clusters in CIELAB color space. It learns from each image locally; it is not a pretrained dermatology model.

02

Review the outline

The edge-dominant cluster estimates background skin color. Color distance, noise filtering, and a connected component around your chosen center propose an outline. You can adjust it and must confirm it.

03

Align and compare

Centroids and principal axes align the masks. Rotation search resolves orientation ambiguity. Equal-area normalization limits differences from camera distance, while also discarding physical size changes.

04

Keep the evidence

The journal stores reviewed photos, measurements, and notes on this device. Export a printable report for a conversation with a clinician. The app never determines urgency or rules out disease.

Evidence & honest limits

The American Academy of Dermatology describes changes in size, shape, or color as observations to discuss with a dermatologist. This prototype documents photo differences; it has not been evaluated for clinical accuracy, diagnostic performance, or performance across skin tones.

Included examples are mathematical test fixtures, not patient photos or evidence of medical effectiveness. Automated checks test identical images, pose changes, shape changes, lighting differences, and rejection paths.
